story866:
Sikakokuh was a boy of the Hopi villages who possessed a hunting dog unlike any other — a creature born with eyes the color of river stones and a spirit that seemed to know things no animal should know. Where other dogs chased rabbits blindly through the mesas, Sikakokuh's dog would pause at the edge of the wash, lift its nose, and point toward exactly where a deer would be standing three valleys away.

The other hunters noticed. They whispered. "How does the boy find game every time?" jealousy poisoned their words like stagnant water. Some began to scheme against the dog, for they believed it carried bad spirits.

But the dog was no ordinary animal. In dreams, it spoke to Sikakokuh in a voice like wind through canyon walls. "When you hunt, you must first offer cornmeal to the earth. You must speak to the spirit of the animal before you draw your bow. If you take without asking, the game will hide from your people forever."

Sikakokuh followed every instruction. He scattered cornmeal at the four directions. He whispered prayers before each hunt. And the deer came willingly, walking toward his arrow as if offering themselves.

One night, a jealous hunter tried to poison the dog with tainted meat. But the spirits of the mountain — the Gahe — intervened. They appeared as masked dancers in the moonlight, their wooden headdresses scraping the stars, and they drove the wicked hunter away into the desert where he wandered for three days without water.

When the hunter returned, broken and repentant, Sikakokuh shared his harvest with him. The dog sat beside them, watching with eyes that held the memory of every hunt, every prayer, every life given so the people might eat.

"The dog is our teacher," Sikakokuh told the village elders. "It shows us that hunting is not conquest. It is conversation."

The story spread through the Hopi villages and became part of the teachings given to young hunters — a reminder that the sacred relationship between human and animal is built on respect, gratitude, and the proper conduct of ceremony.
story875:
In the beginning there was nothing — no earth, no living beings, only darkness, water, and Cyclone the wind. Only the Hactcin existed, spirits of immense power who moved through the void like thoughts through a sleeping mind.

Black Hactcin, the most powerful among them, looked into the darkness and said, "There should be a world." He made the earth as a woman facing upward, her body the landscape itself — her breasts the mountains, her hair the forests, her veins the rivers. He made the sky as a man facing downward, his breath the wind, his voice the thunder.

Then Black Hactcin took clay and shaped the first four-legged animal. He breathed into it and it moved. From its body he made many animals — elk from its shoulders, deer from its haunches, rabbits from its ribs. He made birds from mud mixed with raindrops, giving each one a song appropriate to its size and nature.

The animals and birds gathered before Black Hactcin. "We are alone," they said. "We have no companion who thinks as we think, who speaks as we speak."

Black Hactcin listened. He sent the animals to gather sacred materials — turquoise, coral, opal, jet, abalone, white shell, red stone. From these precious substances he shaped the first man, placing in his chest a spark of his own power.

Four times Black Hactcin commanded: "Speak!" Each time the man spoke, his voice grew stronger. Four times: "Laugh!" Each laugh brought more warmth to his body. Four times: "Shout!" And with the fourth shout, the man was alive.

But the man was lonely. Black Hactcin placed lice in his hair, and the man scratched and slept, and in his sleep he dreamed of a woman. He awoke to find Ancestral Woman beside him, shaped from the same sacred materials but arranged differently — not lesser, not greater, but complementary.

Together they had children, and the people multiplied. They lived in darkness, for the sun and moon had not yet been created. But the Hactcin watched, and they knew the time would come when light would be needed.

The story is told to Hopi children to explain the origin of all living things and the sacred partnership between men and women, between humans and animals, between the visible world and the invisible spirits who shaped it.
story876:
In the Jicarilla Apache emergence story, White God of the East stood at the edge of the underworld and made a mountain that grew toward the sky like a prayer reaching toward the heavens. In the center of the mountain, reeds stood tall and straight, and four girls twisted them until they stopped growing, creating the means of ascent.

Four ladders were made — one black, one blue, one yellow, one variegated like the hide of a wild pony. They were placed at the mountain's four faces, and the people gathered at the base, looking up toward a world they had never seen.

Whirlwind went first, spiraling upward through the layers of rock and soil. When he reached the upper world, he found much water — a world covered in lakes and rivers, still and silent. He called down to the people: "Come! There is a world above, but it needs tending."

Beaver went next. He built dams in the rivers, diverting the water, and where the water receded, land appeared — brown and rich and waiting. Badger followed him, scratching at the soil, and where he dug, plants began to grow.

The people climbed. They started with the black ladder, moving carefully, children carried on their mothers' backs. Then the blue ladder, where they gained the ability to see — though the light of the upper world was painful after so long in darkness. Then the yellow ladder, where they gained speech, their first words clumsy and halting.

The last ladder was variegated, and it stretched the longest. As the people climbed, the ladder began to wear. An old woman and old man, slow with age, could not make the final rungs. They called up to the departing people: "We will stay here. We will become the rulers of the dead."

And so it was established that all who die must pass through the world of the old woman and old man before they can be reborn into the upper world.

The people moved east along four parallel trails, each led by a chief. They traveled for many days until they reached the place near Taos where the great mountain still stands — a reminder of the climb, of the ladders, of the world below that shaped them.
